title: Finite Automata
body:
[[DFA]]s and [[NFA]]s

The bottom rung of the [[Automata]] ladder: a machine with a finite set of states and no
memory beyond which state it is currently in. It reads the input left to right, one symbol at
a time, never goes back, and never writes anything down. When the input runs out it accepts if
it landed in an accepting state.

That is a hard limit, not just a weak design. A finite automaton has $|Q|$ states, so it can
distinguish at most $|Q|$ different histories. Anything that needs unbounded counting, like
matching $n$ opening brackets against $n$ closing ones, is out of reach. Proving that formally
is the job of the [[Pumping Lemma]].

Three descriptions of exactly the same class of [[Languages]], which is the main theorem of
this part of the course:

- [[DFA]], one transition per state and symbol
- [[NFA]], any number of transitions plus $\varepsilon$-moves, converted to a DFA by the
  subset construction
- [[Regular Expressions]], the algebraic notation

Anything all three describe is a [[Regular Languages|regular language]].

This is the same object as the [[Finite State Machine]] in [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]], studied
as mathematics instead of as hardware. There the states live in [[Flip-Flop]]s and the
transition function is [[Sequential Logic|combinational logic]]; here they are just elements
of a set $Q$. Nothing about the theory changes when you solder it.
